summary: A revision of the Mail Box Protocol by the file transfer committee. Mail is limited to ASCII text formatted for a line printer, a new FTP command called Append With Create is added, and a standard mailbox path name is defined. It replaces RFC 221.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC revises an early ARPANET mail delivery protocol. It limits mail to ASCII text formatted for a line printer and defines how a file is appended or created at the destination.

questions: how did early arpanet mail to printers work
what changed in the mail box protocol revision
what does append with create do
what printer dimensions does rfc 278 assume
subtitle: Revises the ARPANET Mail Box Protocol for ASCII text and printer delivery.

tldr.problem: ARPANET hosts needed a defined method for delivering mail text to a remote mailbox or printer.
tldr.mechanism: The revision limits mail items to ASCII text, defines a mailbox pathname and adds an FTP Append With Create operation.
tldr.outcome: RFC 278 replaces RFC 221 and relies on the contemporary File Transfer Protocol.

today: RFC 278 obsoletes RFC 221. It describes a historical ARPANET mail procedure and is not listed as obsoleted in the unit metadata.

sections.title: Changes to the Mail Box Protocol
sections.content:
The file transfer committee confirmed the potential utility of RFC 221's Mail Box Protocol and proposed several changes. The protocol is limited to ASCII text formatted for a network standard line printer.

A new FTP command, Append With Create, appends to a file if it exists and creates it otherwise. The standard mailbox path uses the word MAIL, a separator and either PRINTER or an identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The revision limits mail to printable ASCII text. It also adds a file-transfer operation that can append to an existing mailbox file or create one.

sections.title: Sending a Mail Item
sections.content:
The protocol uses the NCP, Initial Connection Protocol, Data Transfer Protocol and File Transfer Protocol. The sender connects to the standard file transfer socket 3 and sends the mail item as a file.

The basic operation sends an Append With Create request, file data and an end-of-file indication, then receives an acknowledgement. The transmission uses Network ASCII.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender opens the file-transfer connection, sends the mail file and marks its end. The receiving side acknowledges the operation.

sections.title: Printer Format and TIP Delivery
sections.content:
The standard printer is assumed to have a 72-character line and a page of 66 lines. A form feed moves paper to the top of a new page. The sender is responsible for line and page lengths.

The RFC discusses delivery to TIPs, which at that time supported Telnet but were planned to support DTP. The NIC did not plan automatic network delivery to TIPs; messages to TIP users would be delivered to their initial file at the NIC.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender formats the message for the printer's line and page sizes. TIP users receive mail through their NIC file according to the described plan.

references.text: Revision of the Mail Box Protocol, RFC 221, revised by RFC 278.
Telnet Protocol, RFC 158, cited for the line convention.
